source_document.body:
The latest version of the Department of Labor’s (DOL) independent contractor rule was handed down Thursday with minuscule changes from what was proposed in February.
The shift from the Biden administration’s IC rule to that of the second Trump administration is generally viewed as giving the Wage & Hour division of the DOL, in its rulings, guidelines that are more favorable to a finding a worker is an independent contractor rather than an employee.
The IC rule for the Trump 47 administration is not seen as that much different from the rule it implemented in the Trump 45 administration. But that rule didn’t go into effect until Donald Trump was about to leave office.
However, after significant back-and-forth in the court system, it was revived by a court order and was the DOL standard for more than two years before the Biden rule came into effect. That Biden rule is what will be replaced by the Trump 47 rule.
ATA at the ceremony
The final rule is considered positive enough for the trucking industry that the American Trucking Associations ’ new president and CEO Mark Colson took part in what the ATA said was a “celebration” in Washington at the DOL coinciding with the rule’s release.
“A final independent contractor rule issued by the agency will rescind a destructive, Biden-era classification standard,” the ATA said in a prepared statement regarding Thursday’s action.
According to the ATA, both Colson and ATA vice chairman Gregg Troian spoke at the Department of Labor “celebration.”
While there was virtually no criticism coming from the trucking industry about the changes from the Biden rule, which were effectively baked in with the February notice of proposed rulemaking in the Federal Register, a consistent voice in the process has been that of attorney Richard Reibstein, a partner with the firm of Littler Mendelson and an expert on independent contractor status.
How much does it matter?
Throughout the shifts between the Trump and Biden administrations, Reibstein has repeatedly delivered the same message: it’s not that big a deal.
Whatever the DOL came up with “is unlikely to be given deference by the courts, which have historically chosen to apply their own judicial precedent rather than give deference to administrative rules on IC status that change back and forth when a new administration enters the White House,” Reibstein wrote on his blog soon after the IC rule was released Thursday. “Further, most IC misclassification lawsuits as well as agency investigations and proceedings are not brought only under the Fair Labor Standards Act but rather are commenced in whole or in part under state laws, most of which use different tests for IC status.”
Reibstein calculated that the final rule released this week had changed only three sentences and a few additional examples from the proposal of earlier this year.
Today, I’m proud to announce @USDOL has FINALIZED our new INDEPENDENT CONTRACTOR RULE. This Administration is boldly taking the final step toward ENDING UNCERTAINTY by establishing CLEAR and EASY-TO-UNDERSTAND criteria for determining who is an EMPLOYEE and who is an INDEPENDENT… pic.twitter.com/0hxdQeGXqt — Secretary Keith Sonderling (@Sonderling47) November 19, 2026
The final rule will take place 60 days after it is published in the Federal Register.
The trucking industry came in for a notable mention in the almost 400 pages of the rule and its summary, with the DOL citing a lease-purchase agreement as not being a sign of control by the carrier that signs on a driver to such a contract. There had been comments submitted expressing concern over that possibility.
Lease purchase deals are OK
After recapping some of the comments and queries made from trucking interests during the comment period, the DOL said it “generally believes that the fact that a driver owns a truck and exercises initiative in how to operate it seems to plainly indicate independent contractor status under the opportunity for profit or loss factor.”
The DOL said it would specifically add examples in the final rule that deal with a driver operating on a lease purchase agreement that “actually provide an opportunity for the worker to own the vehicle in the future.”
“These facts would indicate independent contractor status under the opportunity for profit or loss,” the DOL said, expecting that there will now be “sufficient clarification in response to a multitude of comments on this topic.”
When the proposed rule was announced in February, a key provision in contrast to the Biden rule was the emphasis on two factors of the “multi-factor economic realities test.”
That wasn’t new; it was part of the 2021 Trump 45 rule that was in effect until 2024.
In reviewing the view of the multi-factor economic realities test, the DOL said the 2021 rule “stated that if these two core factors point towards the same status (i.e., employee or independent contractor), there is a substantial likelihood that the indicated outcome is the worker’s accurate status.
The other three parts of the test that the DOL said are “less probative” and “non-core” are”the amount of skill required for the work, the degree of permanence of the working relationship between the worker and the potential employer, and whether the work is part of an integrated unit of production.”
Those two factors, according to the Scopelitis Law Firm in an email about the rule and its impact on trucking, are “core guideposts which, if aligned in favor of independent contractor status or employee status, will frequently end the analysis.”
Two are more important than the others
But the Biden administration’s rule did not elevate any of the factors above all. That was viewed as making it more likely that the Wage & Hour division or other government agencies relying on the DOL rule would find a worker is an employee rather than an independent contractor.
Scopelitis also noted–as it and others had in February with the proposed rule–that the latest version of the DOL IC rule provided “certainty” on the question of control by “noting that compliance with specific legal obligations and health and safety standards (even voluntary standards) is not control evidencing an employee relationship.”
That had been a key concern under the Biden administration rule whether the employer of an independent owner operator mandating that the driver keep compliant with various regulations was a sign of control, which could undercut any argument that an employee was truly independent.
In a prepared statement, the Owner Operator Independent Drivers Association (OOIDA) expressed mostly support for the final rule.
OOIDA particularly singled out the DOL clarifying that there is no federal rule requiring speed limiters. “DOL’s continued acknowledgement that speed limiters are not a mandated safety device is welcome,” OOIDA said, referring to a footnote that references to a speed limiter in the 2021 rule could have created “potential confusion over whether federal motor carrier safety regulations require the installation of speed limiting devices.”
OOIDA’s endorsement of the rule was not at the level of ebullience of the ATA.
“While the rule does not address all of our concerns, it also does not create new barriers for an owner-operator to work as an independent contractor,” OOIDA said.

Dealer Tried To Scam Senior Subaru Outback Owner, Mechanic Saves the Day
10 photos
Photo: Car Wizard | YouTube
The owner of a 2017 Subaru Outback, a senior driver, took his vehicle to a dealer complaining about an annoying noise that came from under the vehicle. The dealership technicians recommended that he change the radiator and heater hoses. He drove off planning to ask for a second opinion. Now, he should give himself a round of applause for the decision.
The retired owner of the 2017 Subaru Outback wanted to get rid of the annoying rattling that he kept hearing at highway speed and took his vehicle to the dealer. The dealer told the customer he needed all-new radiator hoses and all-new heater hoses, all motor mounts and transmission mounts, which sounded like plenty of spending.
The customer turned suspicious and told the dealership technicians that he wanted a second opinion. This is how he ended up in the shop belonging to David Long, a.k.a. The Car Wizard. He got the Subaru on a lift and checked everything, then told the senior driver that he should keep the money in his pocket.
The hoses are still soft and pliable and by no means need to be replaced. Besides, the maintenance plan does not include that at such low mileage. The nine-year-old Subaru Outback has 21,244 miles on the clock.
Photo: Car Wizard | YouTube His Subaru comes with the 2.5-liter four-cylinder boxer engine, which features the PZEV (Partial Zero Emission Vehicle) technology, produces 175 horsepower and 174 pound-feet of torque. A Lineartronic CVT puts the power down through all four corners.
Nothing seems wrong with the engine. But where does the noise come from, after all? A technician, Clay, took the Subaru out for a spin to figure out the source of the annoying sound that the owner complained about. Driving down a bumpy road, he heard something that sounded like a tin can full of bolts.
The rattling came from the guide pins, the Car Wizard realized. The pins are designed to allow the floating disc brake caliper to slide back and forth smoothly as the driver presses and releases the brake pedal. But they stop working properly when the car drives often on rough terrain or even just a simple dirt road.
The noise gets worse with speed, especially in the 65 - 70 mph (105 - 113 kph) range. When slowing down, the noise reduces. Now it is up to the owner of the Subaru Outback to figure out if the dealership technicians had no idea that it all came down to a tire that was out of balance or just wanted to make more money with a far more complicated procedure.
Photo: Car Wizard | YouTube They recommended replacing hoses, looking for the issue in the wrong area or hiding the real issue the Outback came with. Now, the owner should congratulate himself for looking for a second opinion, it spared him lots of spending.

The Geely Starray EM-I Might Be Your Next Car, Here's What You Need To Know
39 photos
Photo: Naveed Hussain / autoevolution
The Geely Starray EM-i is appropriately named because, like stars in the sky, it is one of many plug-in hybrid SUVs now visible in the UK. It’s the Chinese brand’s second car to reach the UK after the fully electric EX5 , and it faces competition from the Jaecoo 7 , Cherry Tiggo 7 PHEV and BYD Sealion 5. European brands aren’t going down without a fight either, since the Volkswagen Tiguan eHybrid and Ford Kuga plug-in are strong contenders from legacy manufacturers.
The Starray EM-i is powered by a 1.5-litre four-cylinder petrol engine producing 98bhp and a 214bhp electric motor for a combined output of 258bhp. Geely claims 0- 62 mph in 8.0 seconds, putting the Starray EM-i firmly alongside its rivals, with only the more powerful MG HS PHEV and Volkswagen Tiguan eHybrid accelerating faster.
There’s a choice of two battery sizes to go with combustion power: a smaller 18.4kWh unit for a claimed electric-only range of 51 miles, or a larger 29.8kWh battery for up to 84 miles. But don’t think the battery is a side dish, no – it’s the main course, because like the BYD Sealion 5, the Starray EM-i prioritises electric driving to get the most out of EV range, saving petrol for longer journeys. This is kinder to the environment and, ultimately, to your pockets, too.
Driving the Starray EM-i is generally comfortable thanks to the cushiony seats and wafty suspension that soaks up bumps. Acceleration is smooth and more than adequate for most motorists’ needs, with silent driving most of the time, except when the petrol engine cuts in with an unpleasant drone to charge the battery.
The steering is light and responsive, which is great for manoeuvring around town, but it lacks the feedback I’d have preferred. It is, however, slightly too sharp, which is at odds with the relatively comfortable nature of the entire car. It’s a similar problem with the Jaecoo 7 and Cherry Tiggo 7. This means you’ll be finding yourself leaning more into corners during spirited driving.
Use a little extra enthusiasm when exiting a junction on wet tarmac and you can easily spin the wheels. Be delicate, match the car's calmer nature, and you'll find the overall experience pleasant and relaxed. The brakes are strong but rather grabby, and difficult to judge upon first use.
Photo: Naveed Hussain / autoevolution The materials on the inside appear well-made but push and prod a little further and you’ll find room for improvement. The plastics don’t feel as plush as they could, with the centre console flexing when pushed in an earlier test, though my most recent experience has been more positive.
The odd-shaped steering wheel is difficult to ignore, but it’s designed this way so you can see the slender 10.2-inch driver’s display. The buttons on the wheel aren’t intuitive and can often change functions, so it takes a bit of getting used to. The cruise control settings are surprisingly easy to use once you’re accustomed to them.
The infotainment screen is 15.4 inches with sharp graphics and the ability to control a variety of functions such as the climate settings and even the sunshade. I would prefer more physical buttons, but voice assistance comes as standard. Speakers in the headrest are a welcome feature when making phone calls on the go.
The information system isn't the most responsive, and it takes a while to get going when you hop in the driver's seat. My recommendation is to select automatic brightness for the infotainment screen, as it'll be kinder to your eyes and help the ambient lighting really stand out in the Max and Ultra trims. That soft lighting isn’t entirely visible during the day, but sets a lovely mood during nighttime driving – and you can program it to react to your music.
Rear space is a strong point for the Starray EM-i, with plenty of headroom and enough legroom to almost fully stretch your legs out underneath the front seats. The seats are nicely reclined to allow rear passengers to catch a comfortable snooze, and three adults shouldn’t have any problems sitting side-by-side thanks to the flat floor.
Boot capacity is one of the best in the market, with up to 528 litres available. Only the Hyundai Tucson plug-in hybrid beats it with 558 litres. With the seats down, you can expect over 2,000 litres in the Starray EM-i.
Photo: Naveed Hussain / autoevolution There are three trim levels to choose from, starting with the Pro, which comes with the 18.4kWh battery, 19-inch alloy wheels, and a 360-degree surround view camera. The Max adds ambient lighting, a head-up display, a panoramic sunroof and a power tailgate. The Ultra comes with the same standard features as the Max, except it is equipped with the larger 29.8kWh battery. Unless you need the extra range, the Max is the sweet spot in the model range.
Value for money is another key part of the Starray EM-i, as it starts at £29,990 for the entry-level, making it cheaper to buy than the Jaecoo 7 Plug-in hybrid, MG HS PHEV, and significantly cheaper than the Volkswagen Tiguan eHybrid. Only the BYD Sealion 5 can match the Geely on price. For the Max and Ultra trims, you can expect to pay £32,690 and £34,990, respectively.
My cumulative couple of weeks spent with several different variants of the Geely Starray EM-i have helped me understand how well-suited it is for everyday motoring. It offers a comfortable ride around town, plenty of space and practicality, and desirable value for money.

Image: Alpitronic
Alpitronic , the company behind IONNA’s fast chargers, is investing nearly $34 million in a new South Carolina factory. It’ll build 400 kW DC fast chargers, plus a 1 megawatt (MW) system that can charge cars and heavy-duty trucks.
The $33.94 million project in Fort Mill is expected to create 70 jobs, the South Carolina Department of Commerce announced Wednesday. It’ll be the Bolzano, Italy-based Alpitronic’s first operation in South Carolina, just across the state line from its North American headquarters in Charlotte.
What Alpitronic will build in Fort Mill, SC
The HYC400 packs up to 400 kW into a single unit. If you’ve stopped at an IONNA Rechargery, you may have already plugged into one.
The HYC1000 works differently. A separate power cabinet can send up to 1 MW across as many as eight vehicles at once, shifting power between them as their charging needs change. Operators can configure it with CCS or NACS plugs for passenger EVs or a Megawatt Charging System (MCS) plug for compatible heavy-duty trucks.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Alpitronic’s 400 kW chargers were already being made in Wisconsin for Mercedes-Benz High-Power Charging in 2024. Alpitronic Americas CEO Patrik Herrnegger said the Fort Mill plant “will put US production under our direct control, bring us closer to our customers, and enable us to serve them more efficiently.”
The 173,315-square-foot site at 3560 Stateview Blvd. (pictured above) will also house a testing lab, repair operations, a warehouse, logistics space, and offices. South Carolina approved job development credits and awarded York County a $200,000 grant to help pay for building improvements.
Alpitronic expects to start operations in February 2027.

EICMA 2026 • Triumph TF-E Bikes Get Even More Enduro With Updates for the 2027 Model Year
5 Cars That the New James Bond, Robert Pattinson, Should Drive
21 photos
Photo: Amazon | Aston Martin | BMW | JLR | Rolls-Royce | Ferrari
Pattinson. Robert Pattinson. He is the new James Bond that everyone has been debating endlessly over the past three days. The 40-year-old is unlike any 007 before him, since he has already played big roles such as the vampire Edward Cullen in The Twilight Saga and Bruce Wayne in Matt Reeves' The Batman. So, the car he will drive in the upcoming movie might also stray away from the Aston Martins we are used to seeing alongside the secret agent.
Different strokes for different folks, they say. It is always the same. Not all of us liked Daniel Craig playing James Bond, just like not all of us enjoyed watching Pierce Brosnan or Roger Moore (really?) asking for that martini, shaken, not stirred.
All six James Bonds, except Roger Moore, drove Aston Martins in the official 007 films. So will Robert Pattinson get one, too? Well, since Amazon MGM Studios stepped away from the no-star, no-big-role tradition, why wouldn’t they step out of the Aston Martin habit? Let’s see what other options are out there.
1. Jaguar Type 01 The J aguar Type 01 is probably the most controversial arrival of the past ten years, along with Tesla's Cybertruck and Ferrari's Luce. The electric grand tourer has been called everything from "fridge on wheels" to "Cybertruck and Bentley’s illegitimate child."
Photo: JLR Peel off the "toaster-like appearance," and you’ve got a British car with British credentials, just right for the always British James Bond. At 206.1 inches (5,235 millimeters) long and 79.6 inches (2,021 millimeters) wide, and weighing nearly 6,000 pounds (2,722 kilograms), it might not look like the perfect getaway car when the secret agent is trying to escape an ambush.
However, it’s got an ace up its sleeve, and that is acceleration. The Type 01 's tri-motor setup produces 1,015 horsepower (1,030 metric horsepower) and 1,007 pound-feet (1,365 Newton meters) of torque for a run from zero to hero (0 to 60 mph or 0 to 97 kph) in 3.1 seconds and a top speed of 150 mph (241 kph). The 118-kWh battery would let Bond drive as far as 400 miles (643 kilometers), so he won’t need to stop to recharge while chasing perpetrators.
So what is there to really complain about? Yeah, sure, it’s the looks, and James Bond has always driven superb cars from Sean Connery’s Aston Martin DB5 to Daniel Craig's Aston Martin Vantage, but those were different actors, different directors, different screenplay writers, and different visions. That "fridge on wheels" really deserves a chance.
2. BMW M3 CS Handschalter We have seen James Bond driving or traveling in BMWs before. Bond's first non-British Q-Branch car was an Atlanta Blue Z3 roadster outfitted with Stinger missiles, a radar scanner, and a braking parachute. The Z3 showed up in GoldenEye in 1995, starring Pierce Brosnan.
Photo: Cars and Bids Then, we saw the BMW 750iL in 1997 in Tomorrow Never Dies. The sedan can easily be labeled as the most gadget-heavy BMW in the series. The V12-powered BMW featured bulletproof glass, tear gas, caltrops, self-inflating tires, roof-mounted missiles, and a wire cutter hidden under the BMW hood badge. Bond famously drove it from the back seat using a remote-controlled Ericsson cellphone during a parking garage chase.
Then, we got the BMW Z8 in 1999, in The World Is Not Enough. Equipped with titanium armor, remote control via a keychain, and target-tracking missiles hidden in its side vents, the 400-horsepower V8 roadster met one of the franchise’s most memorable fates when a helicopter-mounted buzzsaw sliced it cleanly in half.
Hoping that the 2027 BMW M3 CS Handschalter would have a better fate, the car checks all the right boxes. The inline-six from under the hood pushes out 473 horsepower (480 metric horsepower) and 406 pound-feet (550 Newton meters) of torque.
The car does 0 to 60 in 4.1 seconds on its way to a top speed of 180 mph (290 kph). A six-speed manual transmission, the purists’ favorite, puts the power down through the rear wheels. It’s time James Bond became a car enthusiast.
3. Ferrari Luce Before you boo this car off the stage, hear me out. Sure, it won’t win a beauty pageant, but it’s new, it’s modern, it’s fast, and it follows the "let's save the polar bears" trend. Besides, if we go all controversial with a former Batman/current James Bond, let's go all in.
Photo: Ferrari The Luce is Ferrari's first-ever and probably only electric car in a long time. It comes with a quad-motor setup, capable of churning out 1,035 horsepower (1,050 metric horsepower) and 730 pound-feet (990 Newton meters) of torque. That is good enough for 0 to 60 mph in 2.5 seconds and a top speed of 193 mph (310 kph).
Sure, it’s been called an "iPhone on wheels" and a "Ferrari Multipla," with reference to what was widely regarded as the world’s ugliest car, the first-generation Fiat Multipla. But the Ferrari executives promised it looks better in the flesh than it does in photos .
Fast and quiet, the Ferrari Luce would make a great Bond car. It can glide silently, unlike a V12-powered car that would announce Bond’s arrival from miles away. Besides, it's got the retro-styled yet futuristic cabin that would very well integrate all the gadgets that the secret agent would need.
The roof-mounted control pod, used to engage Launch Control, would double as the exact kind of overhead switch that Bond would flip to deploy smokescreens, oil slicks, or ejector seats. Tactical equipment or a perpetrator with his arms tied and duct tape over his mouth would have enough room in the 21-cubic-foot (600 liters) trunk. Or “boot,” as the British James Bond would call it.
4. Rolls-Royce Spectre Black Badge We're going back to the British roots with the Rolls-Royce Spectre in the shape of the most powerful and quickest car ever built by the British house. Its dual-motor powertrain produces 650 horsepower (659 metric horsepower) and 793 pound-feet (1,075 Newton meters) of torque.
Photo: Rolls-Royce That is enough to make the nearly three-ton luxury coupe flash from 0 to 60 mph in 4.1 seconds on its way to an electronically limited top speed of 155 mph (250 kph). While engaging Infinity Mode unleashes the full potential of the EV, activating the Spirited Mode launch function delivers that full surge of torque for effortless, silent getaways.
Riding on the large 23-inch wheels and equipped with the massive 118.0-kWh (112.4-kWh usable) battery pack, the Spectre Black Badge can drive as far as 308 miles (496 kilometers) before it needs to be plugged in again, which sounds like enough to give the 007 some peace of mind.
Imposing and intimidating, the Spectre Black Badge would be the first Rolls-Royce in the hands of James Bond after decades of being a villain brand. Auric Goldfinger drove a Phantom III in Goldfinger in 1964, Aristotle Kristatos had a Silver Wraith II in For Your Eyes Only in 1981, and Franz Sanchez drove a Silver Shadow in License to Kill in 1989. It is about time Rolls-Royce jumped ship.
5. Aston Martin Valiant Let's get credit where credit is due and not tear to pieces a six-decade-long tradition. Putting the Aston Martin on the list makes perfect sense. Bearing the Q by Aston Martin signature after a personal commission from Formula 1 driver Fernando Alonso, the ultra-limited-run Valiant is based on the Valour .
Photo: Aston Martin Wrapped in carbon fiber, the Valiant is powered by the 5.2-liter twin-turbocharged V12, which produces 735 horsepower (745 metric horsepower) and 555 pound-feet (753 Newton meters) of torque. A true driver’s car, the Valiant comes with a six-speed manual transmission, with exposed gear linkages.
The six-speed puts power down through the rear wheels with the help of a limited slip differential. Don't tell me you don't see James Bond doing some power slides through the winding Alpine passes of Switzerland with a fleet of blacked-out SUVs hot on his tail.
Aston Martin is rolling out only 38 Valiants, and all are already spoken for. Each starts at 2 million pounds, which translates to roughly $2.5 million. Regardless of the price, the Valiant would surely love some screen time in the hands of Pattinson. Robert Pattinson.

Past Owners Lost Interest: Car Nut Saves 1957 Buick Caballero From Field, LS-Swaps It Into Next Year
92 photos
Photo: YouTube/Magnacars
In 1957, Buick looked at the humble station wagon, tossed its B-pillars out the window, and unveiled the Century Caballero Estate Wagon. Naming a 4,423-pound chrome barge after a Spanish horseman felt like strapping ballet slippers onto a grizzly bear, yet the pillarless four-door hardtop looked magnificent. Built for one generation across two model years, Caballero production totaled 14,642 units, comprising 10,186 examples for 1957 and 4,456 for 1958.
From the factory, every 1957 Caballero packed Buick's 364-cubic-inch (6.0-liter) overhead-valve Nailhead V8 with a four-barrel carburetor and 10.0:1 compression, producing 300 horsepower and 400 lb-ft of torque. Buick paired it exclusively with a 2-speed Variable Pitch Dynaflow automatic, adding optional Flight Pitch Dynaflow for 1958 while limiting the 3-speed manual to 250-horsepower Specials. Stock wagons hit 60 mph in 10 to 11 seconds and neared a 110-mph top speed.
If you feel rebellious, sacrilegious, heretic, or simply have a strong desire for moral flailing, mention modifying a rare 1957 Buick. Classic car enthusiasts promptly split into two noisy camps armed with lawn chairs and strong opinions. Purists rightly champion preserving untouched survivors or restoring icons to period-correct glory, safeguarding authentic mid-century engineering, complete with drum brakes that turn panic stops into highly spiritual experiences.
Restomodders, meanwhile, rescue forgotten hulks and blend vintage styling with modern mechanicals and gadgetry, delivering the glorious best of both worlds. Or so they say.
Photo: Instagram/Joel Cannon (@therealdurty30) That intoxicating restomod philosophy rolls into the spotlight on the Magnacars YouTube channel, where host TJ Lamb inspects a wildly engineered 1957 Buick Caballero Estate Wagon built by body-shop owner Joel Cannon. The project began as a true family pursuit after Joel's father, a talented upholsterer, spent 10 years chasing down this exact field-parked wagon before finally phoning his son to announce he had bagged the cruiser.
Yanked directly from that field, the neglected estate wagon underwent a whirlwind build lasting just over one year, followed by roughly 3 years of obsessive refinements, upgrades, and squeak-chasing alongside a handful of helpers. While respecting ubiquitous muscle icons like the 1969 Camaro, Joel refused to build another clone. Having previously owned cramped two-seat roadsters, he wanted an unmistakable family hauler for taking his two kids to shows and ice cream.
Well, he got the show part right. We can’t say he nailed it in the head, because the Nailhead is not part of this build.
Photo: YouTube/Magnacars Outside, Joel brokered a mischievous peace treaty between preservation and customization by leaving Mother Nature's sun-baked patina untouched and un-clearcoated across the upper body while repairing the rockers and cleanly refinishing the lower two-tone section. He subtly chopped the roof, swapped bright chrome for warm nickel plating, fitted new side glass while babying the rare original rear window, and 3D-printed roof-rack stanchions after the pot metal crumbled.
Underneath that gloriously weathered disguise lies an all-General Motors hardware raid thorough enough to make a parts counter clerk break into a cold sweat. Joel grafted the complete independent rear suspension cradle from a wrecked 2018 Chevrolet Camaro 1LE beneath the tailgate, pairing it with sixth-generation Chevrolet Corvette front control arms and massive brakes.
Skipping airbags, hydraulic-over-coilover units adjust ride height 5 inches while maintaining permanent, composed coilover suspension dynamics.
Photo: YouTube/Magnacars Climb inside, and the chronological whiplash could launch a concours judge's clipboard straight into orbit. The seats and center console migrated from that same wrecked 2018 Camaro 1LE, stripped of headrests, reshaped, and reupholstered by Joel's father in monochromatic blue with Cerakote brown accents. Heated and cooled seats, Kenwood navigation with backup camera, Focal audio, BBT Fab handles, a Sparks Industries billet wheel, and 3D-printed ZL1 Wagon badges modernize everything.
Lifting the hood unveils the crown jewel behind Joel's ZR1 Wagon nickname, though the mechanical recipe is craftier than a simple engine transplant. Power comes from a 6.2-liter GM LS3 V8 upgraded with a Brian Tooley Racing camshaft and backed by a 6-speed automatic transmission featuring Tiptronic shifting. Perched atop sits a genuine sixth-generation Corvette ZR1 supercharger bought through a GM dealer, adapted via a Lingenfelter drive kit for 583 wheel horsepower.
Before receiving forced induction, the all-aluminum 6.2-liter LS3 proved itself across GM's performance stable, powering over 82,000 C6 Corvettes between 2008 and 2013, plus the Camaro SS, Pontiac G8 GXP, and Chevrolet SS. Stock naturally aspirated C6 versions made 430 horsepower and 424 lb-ft of torque, or 436 horsepower with dual-mode exhaust, rocketing to 60 mph in 4.0 seconds, running a 12.4-second quarter-mile at 116 mph, and reaching 190 mph.
Photo: YouTube/Magnacars Meanwhile, the Eaton TVS R2300 supercharger crowning Joel's wagon originally belonged to Chevrolet's ferocious 2009 through 2013 C6 Corvette ZR1, a flagship limited to 4,684 units across 5 model years. Mounted atop the hand-built 6.2-liter LS9 V8 rated at 638 horsepower and 604 lb-ft of torque, it hurled the ZR1 to 60 mph in 3.4 seconds, ran an 11.3-second quarter-mile at 131 mph, and achieved a 205-mph top speed.
On the road with TJ Lamb riding shotgun, even half-throttle stabs make the heavy long-roof wiggle for grip while unleashing a menacing supercharged roar that seems comically unhinged emerging from a sun-faded 1957 station wagon. Heated seats hum, handling stays taut, and passing traffic takes barely an ankle twitch. Appraised at roughly $347,000, the finished wagon heads to Barrett-Jackson in Arizona in January as Joel eyes his next creative build.
Ultimately, classic motoring needs both sides of this lively fence to stay vibrant. Unmolested survivors and factory-exact restorations deserve fierce protection as rolling time capsules, preserving every quirky Dynaflow sigh and whitewall wobble for future generations. Yet when a forgotten field carcass gets resurrected like Joel's Caballero, restomod culture proves its magic, letting a 69-year-old Buick haul kids and humiliate modern sports cars before the ice cream even melts.

EICMA 2026 • MTPeak Stole Some of the Spotlight at EICMA 2026 With Insane Power and Retro Looks on Three Wheels
Assetto Corsa Rally 0.7 Feels Like Driving in a Winter Wonderland
47 photos
Photo: autoevolution
I don’t know about you, but everyone in my social media feed seems to be enjoying GTA IV after its official debut less than 24 hours ago. Well, some have just hopped aboard the hype train by using visual cues or songs from the game, and it’s impossible to look away at least for a few days.
I haven’t gotten the game, but I was curious to read my colleague's take on the subject and also see his first game play session. I’m not 100% sure I want to get it too, for two reasons. Firstly, I think the series reached its peak with San Andreas and I had blast playing it almost 20 years ago. And secondly, I’ve become way more obsessed with cars and motorsports than ever before. That means I was eagerly waiting for the 19th of November for a different kind of virtual event: Assetto Corsa Rally’s Update 0.7!
Update 0.6 arrived in September, allowing us to experience the Audi Quattro Gr.4, the Peugeot 206 WRC, and the Volkswagen Polo GTI R5 . The last time we got a new stage in the game was back in June with Update 0.5, when Rally Greece became available to everyone who joined the Early Access phase of Supernova’s rally-focused title. Just last month, I had a chat with AC Rally’s Director (Irvin Zonca), which provided some exciting insights into the work the team is engaged in for the future of it all.
And if you’ve been following the developer’s official accounts, you may have already been aware of Update 0.7 was all about. I couldn’t wait to test the new 1986 Lancia Delta S4: it’s one of my all-time favorite Group B rally cars! The engine sits behind the driver, and uses both a turbocharger and supercharger for an output of 450 hp. It’s not just that, but it also weighs 950 kg, whereas a “regular” Delta Integrale Evoluzione is quite a bit heavier while also having access to less power.
The Delta S4 is the fifth Lancia in AC Rally , as we already had access to the aforementioned Delta, the Fulvia Coupe HF 1600, the Stratos HF 1976 and the Rally 037 Evo 2. I’m by no means a rally expert, and I’ve had a tough time navigating through the simplest of stages in the Stratos and 037 because of their layouts. I was worried I’d struggle just as much with the Delta S4, but was too excited about finally experiencing it in this game to begin with.
There’s an even faster Lancia Delta S4 Photo: autoevolution It has been a while since I could last enjoy AC Rally, and I was always start off in Livigno for a proper warm-up session. I had a hard time adjusting to it, and I’ve yet to figure out a way to deal with AC Rally cars that have a rear-mounted engine. I needed 67 seconds for my fastest lap, which is way slower than I have been able to achieve in some of the WRC spec machines in the game. However, I knew I couldn’t come up with a valid conclusion before taking it out on a gravel stage.
As my friends from Greece recently showed me some cool shots from the Acropolis Rally , I’m 99% certain I want to go there next year. And I’m thankful I can just experience it anytime I want, even if it’s just virtually, by using my PC. I opted for the shorter, New Loutraki stage, which is only about 4 km long. I expected a disaster, and I got the complete opposite. “We” got along so much better in the gravel, and I only needed four minutes to finish the stage despite making several mistakes.
The Delta S4 is a master of negotiating both the technical and high speed sections, and I only have one complaint: I’d like a louder supercharger please! I had forgotten all about the Evo2 Italtecnica 2021 version of the Delta S4 , and I can see how including it in this update was an easy decision for the studio. It weighs just as much as its older “sibling”, but comes with 250 hp more horsepower and also more torque. It felt easier to drive in Livigno, up until the point where I parked it on its roof.
I was only one second faster overall around the short, icy track, and I once again didn’t know what to expect from the main rally stage. I’d say terrifying is good word for it, especially if you’re still struggling to keep up with your copilot pace notes. It was a bit too intense for me for now, and it’s no wonder the developers mentioned it’s recommended for pros! Also, I was halfway through the stage when I realized I initially expected to see the road-going version of the Delta S4 in the game.
Rally Sweden has arrived! Photo: autoevolution Sure, it would have been slower, but it would probably still been enough to increase your heartbeat after a few corners. The other big news for Update 0.7 is that Rally Sweden is joining the roster, with two locations, 14 stages and about 18 miles/30 km of driving exclusively through the snow. At first, that sounded like paradise to me, as I love going sideways in those conditions. But I quickly realized how little room for error there is on this stages, with massive snow banks left and right.
It’s a true winter wonderland, there’s no doubt about that. I know Update 0.7 has brought some changes in the physics department, and my arms soon started to hurt from the excessive force feedback. Not only that, but at least five items dropped off my desk from the vibrations which is why I had to tone it down a bit. My first impression is that Vargasvagen is the most difficult rally stage I’ve ever experienced, and you can easily tell just by looking at some of the photos of the Peugeot WRC just before the finish line.
It took me 14 minutes to cover 11 miles/ 18 km, and I think I might have to stick to “cruise speed” for a little while longer to get used to the conditions. Going for Gravendal West at night with a snow blizzard activated was quite “smart”. The level of immersion is incredible, and I’m still shocked by how good the environment looks like. I had fun for a while in my Audi Quattro , at least until I destroyed my headlights which left me unable to see anything ahead.
Update 0.7 also features the new Online Rally Weekend Mode which will allow you to compete in some special stages and improve your rally skills. There are quite a few more changes and fixes, and I’m sure Rally Sweden will keep most of us entertained for the next two or three months before Update 0.8 comes along. Why do I feel like dedicating my entire life to rallying every time I play this game?

The List of the North American Car of the Year Is Here, and There Is No Ford
10 photos
Photo: Kia | Lexus | Mercedes-Benz | GM | Nissan | Ram Trucks
Twelve vehicles are still running for the 2027 North American Car, Truck and Utility Vehicle of the Year Award. Ford has no representative in the race in any of the three categories after the Maverick Lobo went home with the Truck of the Year Award in 2026. So, place your bets, ladies and gentlemen!
There are three models in each category trying to steal the show and snatch the award. The names of the lucky short-listed models were revealed at the Los Angeles Auto Show.
In the passenger car segment, the budget-friendly Kia K4 Hatchback , the refined Lexus ES, and the electrified Mercedes-Benz CLA 220 Hybrid are battling for the North American Car of the Year title, offering three very different takes on the modern daily drive
In the meantime, the truck category lacks a very important player, leaving the door open after Ford’s six-year winning streak. That is because the Blue Oval is still over a year away from the next-generation F-150, while a new-gen Ranger won’t be here before 2030.
Photo: Kia This means that the all-new Chevrolet Silverado 1500 and its sibling, the GMC Sierra 1500, are left to battle Ram’s pride and joy, the supercharged HEMI-powered 1500 SRT TRX. Packing massive V8 punch, the 777-horsepower TRX stands as the most powerful truck with a combustion engine currently on the market, pitting raw off-road performance against GM's freshly redesigned workhorses.
In the North American Utility Vehicle of the Year category, an American-made SUV is battling two Asian models in an all-electrified showdown. The compact electric Kia EV3, the hybrid Nissan Rogue e-POWER , and the highly anticipated Rivian R2 boxy crossover are all in for the win.
This year, there is a new category. The North American Automotive Technology of the Year Award will go home with the model that features specific hardware or software features in production vehicles that meaningfully improve safety, convenience, usability, or overall vehicle functionality.
For the inaugural year, the juries have voted for Rivian's Adaptive Drive Beam, Volkswagen’s Emergency Assist Plus, and Volvo’s Multi Adaptive Safety Belt, highlighting the importance of practical advancements designed to protect drivers and other road users.

Who doesn’t love a good fastback? BYD’s new Han was spotted completely undisguised, giving us an early look at its sleek design and interior ahead of its expected debut next week.
BYD updates the Han with a new style and tech
After launching the flagship Great Han last month, or the “Da Han,” as it’s called in China, BYD is preparing to introduce another new member to the lineup.
BYD already sells the smaller Han, but the electric sedan is due for an overhaul. The new version appeared in a regulatory filing by China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) last month.
According to the filing, the next-generation BYD Han will be available in three battery electric (BEV) and one plug-in hybrid (PHEV) variants.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The Han EV will offer two single-motor rear-wheel-drive (RWD) options, with an output of 328 hp (245 kW) and 402 hp (300 kW). A dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) version will also be offered, delivering a combined 697 hp (520 kW).
All variants use BYD’s Blade LFP Battery and are expected to be equipped with its five-minute Flash Charging technology.
The PHEV version, on the other hand, uses a 1.5-liter engine and an electric motor with up to 268 hp (200 kW).
BYD’s new Han spotted without camouflage (Source: Autohome)
Ahead of its expected debut at the Guangzhou Auto Show on November 27, BYD’s new Han was captured in public without any disguise.
The images sent to Autohome show a design similar to the Great Han and other new Dynasty series vehicles, with its latest “Dragon Face” signature front-end look.
A few things have changed from the current model, including new headlights and a full-length light bar, while the Chinese symbol moved to the hood.
BYD’s new Han spotted (Source: Autohome)
From the side, the Han features a sleek, fastback silhouette. The vehicle also features a roof-mounted LiDAR to support advanced driver-assistance features. The new Han is expected to feature BYD’s God’s Eye B ADAS system.
Inside, the new Han adopts BYD’s updated interior design. The new setup includes a floating center infotainment screen and a digital instrument panel behind a three-spoke steering wheel.
BYD’s new Han interior (Source: Autohome)
The center console is also updated with two wireless phone chargers and cupholders without covers.
BYD’s new Han is 5,156 mm long, 1,969 mm wide, and 1,507 mm tall, with a wheelbase of 3,030 mm, which is 161 mm longer than the current version.
The flagship Great Han is the largest of the series, measuring 5,256 mm long. After launching the Great Han on October 13, BYD sold 4,000 units by November 1.
Since the flagship sedan starts at 235,900 yuan, or about $35,000, the smaller Han will likely be closer to 200,000 yuan ($30,000) or less. The outgoing Han starts at 168,800 yuan ($25,000).

source_document.body:
EICMA 2026 • Yamaha Previews the Future of the Tenere Adventure Bikes With Mysterious 4 Concept
New 2027 Toyota RAV4 Cabrio Lowers Its Roof in Fantasy Land
12 photos
Photo: Screenshot Youtube | AutoYa
The sixth-generation Toyota RAV4 will blow one candle off its birthday cake next month, as production kicked off back in December 2021.
It is currently put together not only in its local market of Japan, but also in Canada, as well as in the United States, and China. It’s based on the TNGA-K platform, just like the Camry, Highlander BEV, Crown Sport, Grand Highlander, Lexus LM, TX, TZ, NX, RX, Subaru Getaway, and other models, and as every petrolhead and their pet could tell you, it is offered in a single body style: a five-door SUV.
Could a second body style potentially join the new-gen Toyota RAV4 family? If you had asked us a few decades ago, we would have said yes. That’s because three-door versions, both with fixed-roof and convertible designs, were still a thing back then. However, given that these models are not that popular in today’s automotive world, the answer is definitely no. So, no matter how nicely you may ask the company for a different body style of the latest RAV4, they will politely decline.
Photo: Screenshot Youtube | AutoYa But if such a thing is not in the making, nor even on the table, then what is up with the one pictured above in the gallery? As mentioned in the title, it lives in Fantasy Land. Thus, it is a mere rendering take on a potential open-top version of the model, which came via AutoYa on YouTube, where it was recently uploaded. The pixel artist imagined it from several angles, painted in different colors, and the cockpit is also visible in some of the digital illustrations.
Compared to the real sixth-gen Toyota RAV4, this imagined RAV4 Convertible has shorter front and rear overhangs, and a lot less space between the axles. It is also not that tall, and features an open-top view of the sky above, with a folding rag top that sits behind the rear seats when folded down. It also sports a full-size spare wheel attached to the rear door, has much thicker B-pillars, a cramped back seat with room for three occupants, and the same overall layout as the real one, albeit on a smaller scale.
It definitely has an adventurous spirit, and this thing would feel right at home in certain parts of the world. For what it’s worth, I am definitely a fan of the design, as unlike other open-top crossovers that have been launched over the years, this one is actually good to look at. Too bad Toyota does not intend to build such a thing, because a new-gen RAV4 Convertible would probably sell in sufficient numbers to justify the investment. But would you buy such a model if it were real, or would you simply ignore it?
